How a cow town in Alabama became an R&D capital
Why physics travels but social science must be homegrown

brief.head: Patents tell all
brief.text: A patent buys 17 years of exclusivity, Ajay Shah said, but it is really a disclosure document, spelling out the invention so others can replicate it. {#patents}

brief.head: One rupee, three
brief.text: Every rupee the government raises costs about three rupees of GDP, Ajay Shah and Vijay Kelkar have argued, so spending must earn society three. {059-C04}

brief.head: Five things, done well
brief.text: The scarcest thing in the world, Ajay Shah said, is leadership’s time and attention. A leadership doing only five things would get them done better. {059-C03}

brief.head: Detach from the tribe
brief.text: India must grow its own social scientists, Ajay Shah said, able to study their society coldly, without advocacy. “I’m just here to study this country.” {059-C07}

brief.head: Goosebumps, 1958
brief.text: Ajay Shah called the 1958 Science Policy Resolution, quoted at length in the paper, “goosebumps material”, though its dreams now need new methods. {059-R05}

thought.text: If there is no possibility of failure, it’s not research.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, explaining why governments, which hate failure, should contract research out

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the state and innovation
lead.head: Hire the lab, don’t build it
body: Should the Indian state spend money to make innovation happen at all? Amit Varma and Ajay Shah argued about that for much of the episode. On how it should go about it, if it must, they ended up agreeing.

The occasion was a paper by Shah with the scientist RA Mashelkar and Susan Thomas, *Rethinking innovation policy in India*. Varma, who finds most academic papers turgid, praised its “clear language”. {059-R01}

Shah started from freedom. Left alone, he said, a society will innovate by itself. But knowledge leaks, through publications, patents, machines that can be reverse-engineered, and people talking to friends.
“So the total gain to society may be 100, but only 40 is captured by me,” Shah said. Each firm therefore underinvests in research, and that market failure is the case for the state. {059-C01}

Varma was not convinced. The state runs on coerced taxes, he argued, so its every act carries a moral cost, and positive externalities can be found almost everywhere. Pointing to one is not enough. {059-C02}
## The case for contracting

On what to fund, they agreed. India should free-ride gratefully on knowledge made abroad, Shah said, and spend public money only on problems nobody else will solve, such as COVID in hot, humid Indian homes. {059-C06}

Then came the heart of the paper. Like a company choosing between its own canteen and a caterer, the state can “make” research in vertical organisations such as ISRO, DRDO and CSIR, or “buy” it from universities and firms. {#canteen}
Making defeats the purpose, Shah argued, because the spillovers stay sealed inside the state. “Our objective is not to make the Indian state great, our objective is to make India great.” {059-C08}
Buying also suits research, which needs rival pathways and the freedom to fail. Inside government, Shah said, approvals lock onto one path and auditors treat failure as wrongdoing. {059-C09}
Varma was won over on the how. Spreading research across universities and firms, he said, produces exactly what the title of a Matt Ridley talk describes: *When Ideas Have Sex*. {059-J19}
## Doubts and a blueprint

His worries were about India. American examples rest on invisible infrastructure, such as the rule of law, Varma said, while Indian scholars wait years for grant money: “our invisible infrastructure is invisible because it is non-existent.” {059-J04}
Why would officials give up budgets and subordinates? Change must come from the top, Shah said, borrowing from Vijay Kelkar: “the politicians are the entrepreneurs”. {059-C11}

The paper sketches a 20-year path: new chapters in the General Financial Rules allowing grants and cost-plus contracts, founding documents that require contracting out, and teams that mix science, engineering and law. {059-C12}

Reform one or two of the five big science organisations that matter, Shah said, and start one or two new ones, among them an Indian NIH and a DARPA-like agency. “So we’re not proposing an upheaval, we’re proposing a 20 year journey.”
## Long games
Varma held his ground on the why, recommending Matt Ridley’s *How Innovation Works*, a bottom-up account of innovation whose author, he thought, would agree with much of his scepticism. {059-R02}

Shah’s own pick was Huntsville, Alabama, a cow town seeded with German rocket scientists. It echoed, he said, an old Gandhian idea: people who each dug into a single village after independence. A few remarkable people in one place, he said, are “disproportionately powerful once you’re willing to play for the long term”. {059-S09}

second.label: Knowledge spillovers
second.head: Mum’s not the word
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why Israel’s engineers talk and Apple’s stay silent
body: Nobody outside Apple knows what it will announce next. In Silicon Valley, Ajay Shah said, non-disclosure agreements and a commercial culture keep employees’ mouths shut: a low-spillover environment. {059-S02}

Israel is the opposite. “It is said of the glorious Israeli innovation ecosystem that the scientists and the engineers are blabber mouths,” he said. Nearly all of them went through conscription, often with real fighting, and the friendships formed there cut across company lines.

Every firm’s knowledge leaks quietly to others through networks of army buddies, Shah said, and the same happens in India. That is why firms capture only part of what their research is worth, and why they spend too little on it. {059-C01}

quote.text: If you don’t lock up people in a vault in the desert, then there will be knowledge spillovers.

second.caption: Israel’s blabbermouth engineers

third.head: From Tata to the state
body: Two of the proudest names in Indian science, TIFR and BARC, began as private projects of the Tata group, Ajay Shah reminded listeners. After independence they were handed to the Union government, which paid for everything and made their staff civil servants. {059-S01}
That “make” template was repeated across the ICMR, ICAR, DRDO, CSIR and ISRO: vertical government organisations, often sited away from the main centres of economic activity, building things in-house.
They can do remarkable things. They sent a craft to orbit Mars, Shah said, at a claimed total cost lower than that of the film *The Martian*. {#martian}
Shah does not second-guess the choices made after 1947. “Maybe that was the only way available then,” he said. His question is whether today’s India needs a different model.
third.caption: the Tata origins of TIFR and BARC

p2.title: Make or buy
p2.deck: How the state should fund science: Ajay Shah’s paper, and Amit Varma’s doubts about it

sections.label: The why
sections.head: Ideas leak, so firms skimp
sections.caption: why ideas leak
body: Left to itself, Ajay Shah said, a free society will set about building knowledge and innovating. “People will do it.” The question, as always, is whether there is a market failure. {#default}

There is, he said, and it is the same one that affects higher education: knowledge spillovers. Publications get read, patents spell out inventions in full, and machines can be reverse-engineered and copied.
A lab of total secrecy is possible in theory, Shah said, but in reality knowledge always spills over. People talk. “That’s called community.”
If society gains 100 from an innovation and the innovator keeps only 40, he said, every firm will underinvest. {059-C01}
## Closing the gap

The remedy is for the state to raise taxes and spend them in ways that create high spillovers, so that knowledge diffuses through society. Shah’s rough numbers for India: if 100 is the right level of spending and firms are at 60, the government could fill the gap of 40. {#sixty}
Such questions, he said, deserve first principles rather than a default of “Oh, yeah, science is very good” and more money for government labs.
~ The money comes at a price. The government, Shah said, “uses violence, it uses coercion” to extract taxes. That was where Amit Varma’s objections would begin.

quote.text: So each individual, each firm tends to underinvest in innovative activities, and that’s the market failure.

sections.label: The first doubt
sections.head: Seen, unseen and taxed
sections.caption: the cost of state action
body: Amit Varma’s first objection went to the root. “Every act of government is an act of violence,” he said, the headline of a column he once wrote: the state exists on taxes raised by coercion. {059-R08}

Political philosophies, he argued, differ mainly on when that violence is justified. {059-C02} Positive externalities can be found in almost anything, so innovation ranks below rule of law, defence and basic infrastructure.

Ajay Shah was “very sympathetic”. Every rupee the government raises, he and Vijay Kelkar have argued, costs about three rupees of GDP, through collection, compliance and the way people change their behaviour to avoid tax. {059-C04}
## Who pays, who gains

Varma took the test as necessary but not sufficient. He cited Suyash Rai’s argument against demonetisation: when one set of people bears the costs and another gets the benefits, it is immoral to point to society’s overall gain.
Shah argued that Nehru-era science and higher education seeded India’s IT industry. Varma, borrowing Frédéric Bastiat’s phrase, called that the seen. {059-J10}

~ The unseen, he said, was what the money would have done had it stayed with the poor it was taken from, and a top-down mindset that kept hundreds of millions in poverty for decades longer than necessary. {059-C05}

quote.text: Everybody pays taxes. Even the beggar at the traffic signal has to buy salt, and there is a tax on that.

sections.label: The what
sections.head: Free-ride, and say thank you
sections.caption: what India should leave to the world
body: A poor country need not invent semiconductors, Amit Varma said; it can free-ride on innovation elsewhere. Ajay Shah agreed, with gratitude. “It is the grace of the world that creates all this knowledge, and we are the beneficiaries.” {059-C06}

The transistor, Unix and thermodynamics were not invented in India, Shah said. Cheap solar panels exist thanks to Chinese factories and research in Europe, America and Japan, and Covishield, from Oxford and AstraZeneca, was paid for abroad.
## What only India will do
But some problems nobody abroad will solve. How does COVID spread in Indian heat and humidity, in open homes with fans? How do you fly drones at 18,000 feet in Ladakh? {#ladakh}

Vaccines for malaria and chikungunya will have to be made here, Shah said, and so will much of the humanities and social sciences. He recalled a line he thinks was Heisenberg’s: every electron is the same, and every love is different. {059-J11}
Varma saw this as the converse of subsidiarity: take everything you can from the world, and build at home only what it won’t give you. {#converse}
~ Told that India’s mosquitoes change every two hundred kilometres, Varma argued it was less, and recalled writing a limerick on the mosquitoes of Versova for the *Times of India*. {#limerick}

quote.text: So there is a whole zone in which free riding is good and wise.

sections.label: The how
sections.head: Back more than one horse
sections.caption: make versus buy
body: Every organisation chooses between making and buying, Ajay Shah said. A company can run its own canteen or hire a caterer, and then police the contract with random tests for bacteria and gutter oil. {#canteen}

Indian science has been made: civil servants in ISRO, DRDO or CSIR crafting “some cool toys inside the government”. Buying means contracting universities, public or private, and firms. Shah has “absolutely no concern” whether it is Ashoka University or IIT Madras.
There, PhD students carry knowledge out, teaching spreads it and firms find civilian uses. {059-C08}
## The freedom to fail

Research is risk, Shah said, and government hates risk. Approval processes lock onto one path, insiders snuff out rivals, and auditors cannot accept failure. “How will you explain to the CAG that we failed?” {059-J03}

Contract out, and the state can fund six rival teams for a COVID vaccine and double down on the two that work. {#six} Even a telescope on the moon, he argued, would get there cheaper and faster by buying.
~ Amit Varma bought the method but not the moon. Landing a craft there, he said, is propaganda a poor country should not pay for; eradicating malaria would make the better example. {#malaria}

quote.text: Research is risk taking, it is raw risk taking, it is peering into the future and not knowing what will happen.

sections.label: The way forward
sections.head: Plant the sapling now
sections.caption: the 20-year blueprint
body: Amit Varma’s remaining doubts were about India. NASA, he said, citing the paper, sees some five fraud cases in twenty-five thousand contracts. {#fraud} In India, contracting out could become a gravy train for cronies.

Ajay Shah agreed these problems cannot be solved quickly. Space excellence, he argued, is really contracting excellence: the American equivalents of India’s General Financial Rules made NASA possible. {059-C10}
Officials will not give up their budgets willingly, he said, but leaders can push change, as the Vajpayee period showed with the National Highways Authority of India.
## Three pillars

The paper offers “drafting instructions”: new chapters in the rules for grants and cost-plus contracts, founding documents that make contracting out the job, and manuals and teams that mix science, engineering and law. {059-C12}
India has tried before. NMITLI, at CSIR, gave private firms money and CSIR’s knowledge to turn innovations into products, and ran successfully for some years. {#nmitli} It is no more.
~ Nobody expects this overnight, Shah said. He quoted Larry Summers: if a tree will take 20 years to grow, run outside and plant the sapling right now. {#summers}

quote.text: To become a great successful country in space research, what you need is amazing levels of capability on how to do government contracting.

side.boxText: *Rethinking innovation policy in India: Amplifying spillovers through contracting-out*, by RA Mashelkar, Ajay Shah and Susan Thomas, argues that the state should buy research rather than make it. Amit Varma, who doubts its why, recommended it himself. {059-J06}

contQuote.text: Whereas if universities and private firms know about nanotechnology, then that knowledge spills over and it becomes material for the entire country, for the entire economy, and we as a people become better off.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Rockets, fighters, highways and a cow town: how the state gets science done

stories.start: The first example is NASA. Okay. Everybody loves NASA right from its inception
stories.end: goes out to private universities, government universities, and private companies
stories.caption: how NASA contracts out
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the contracting machine behind NASA
stories.head: The space agency that buys
body: NASA dates, Ajay Shah thinks, from 1958. From its founding paragraphs, he said, it was warned against hiring its own people and building things, and told to contract out instead. {#nasa1958}

It still defends its budget that way. Give NASA 100 rupees, it tells lawmakers, and 80 go out to universities and private firms. “Only 20% of the money that goes to NASA stays inside NASA, 80% goes out as contracts,” Shah said. {059-S03}

The contracting comes in stages, by technology readiness level. Rival universities and firms first write early concepts; then come design documents, then working demos tested in NASA’s office, and finally production orders, such as five of a particular engine.

When integrated circuits arrived, NASA was effectively their only buyer, because spacecraft needed miniaturisation while circuit boards on Earth could stay bulky. All the early chip firms ran on NASA contracts. “When the IC came along, it was NASA that smelled blood,” Shah said. {059-S04}

Then there is the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, the control room for NASA’s interplanetary missions to Mars and Jupiter. It is not a government facility. It is a long-term contract, housed since the 60s at Caltech, a private university. {059-S05}

Most people in India, Shah said, would be shocked to learn this. Caltech, he said, is one of the world’s great engineering universities. Thousands of JPL staff sit beside its researchers, and coffee-table conversations help both.
~ “What happens in NASA doesn’t stay in NASA,” Amit Varma said. {059-J08}
stories.why: NASA’s greatness, in Shah’s account, is largely a contracting machine. Sending most of its money out builds capability across the country, has seeded an industry and makes the budget easier to defend. {059-C10}

stories.start: At the end of the Second World War, the Soviets and the Americans
stories.end: filled with cows and peasants, in three generations, it turns into magic
stories.caption: Huntsville, Alabama
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s oddball recommendation: a town in Alabama
stories.head: Rocket men in cow country
body: Asked for a recommendation, Ajay Shah offered a place: Huntsville, Alabama. After the Second World War, he said, the Americans and the Soviets raced across occupied Europe for the German scientists behind the V-1 and V-2 missiles.

Many were diehard Nazis who could not be trusted loose in society. So the American military dumped them in an obscure corner of America, kept them in semi-imprisonment for a time and built them a lab. This was “make not buy”, Shah noted.

The scientists put down roots and raised families. Their children landed up in school, competed with the locals and drove up standards, and over a couple of generations the hick town became one of the world’s great R&D capitals. {059-S08}
~ Amit Varma hoped the story was not leading to a normative place: “Let’s find 200 Nazis and round them up.” {059-J05}
stories.why: Talent compounds when planted in one place, Shah argued: seed a town with a few remarkable people and give it generations. Gandhians who each dug into a single village showed the same thing. {059-S09}

stories.start: The third example in the paper is French military RD.
stories.end: being funded by the government in private corporations in the French military system
stories.caption: French military R&D
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah takes the case outside the English-speaking world
stories.head: Private jets, French style
body: Every military, Ajay Shah said, must do some research of its own to adapt its equipment. Can you put modern night vision on an old T72? {#t72} In India that work is done the “make” way, through DRDO.

France does it differently. The bulk of its military research and production is done by corporations. The military sets the challenge, “I want ABCD capabilities”, and private firms do the research under government contracts.
Rafale is a great French fighter, Shah said. “It is built in the private sector. It is designed in the private sector.” {059-S06}
~ The French use a cost-plus contract, he said, which is not a grant but effectively pays for the private firm’s risk-taking.
stories.why: Even defence can be bought rather than made, in Shah’s account, if the law can share risk. India’s General Financial Rules, he said, have no concept of grants or cost-plus contracts. {#gfr}

stories.start: In terms of a practical demo of precisely this kind of change, I offer
stories.end: NHAI has not yet learned how to properly do PPP highways
stories.caption: how NHAI was built
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s answer to officials who won’t let go
stories.head: The road less built
body: Why would officials who control budgets and staff ever give work away? Amit Varma asked. Change, Ajay Shah said, comes from politicians, not officials. {059-C11}

India’s highways used to be built by the Public Works Department. In the Vajpayee period, Shah said, the leadership decided the government should give out contracts to private builders instead, and the National Highways Authority of India was built for it. {059-S07}
From the ground up, NHAI was a “buy” organisation. “It doesn’t have the engineers who will go make a road,” Shah said. Its engineers and lawyers write contracts instead.
~ It is far from finished, he said: NHAI has still not learned how to do PPP highways properly. But the shift happened, because at the leadership level “people got the point”.
stories.why: Structural reform of the Indian state is possible once leaders grasp the idea, Shah argued. It takes generations, but India already has a working precedent for exactly this kind of transition.

quiz.q: Which two flagship institutions of Indian science began as private projects of the Tata group?
quiz.a: TIFR and BARC, handed to the Union government after independence.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s example, if society gains 100 from an innovation, how much does the innovator capture?
quiz.a: Only 40, which is why private firms underinvest in innovation.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, are Israel’s scientists and engineers said to be blabbermouths?
quiz.a: Conscription: army friendships cut across firms, so knowledge leaks through networks of buddies.

quiz.q: Which private university houses NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, the control room for interplanetary missions?
quiz.a: Caltech, under a long-term NASA contract that has run since the 60s.

quiz.q: Which Indian organisation does Ajay Shah offer as proof that the state can switch from make to buy?
quiz.a: The National Highways Authority of India, set up in the Vajpayee period.

quiz.q: Which French fighter, according to Ajay Shah, was designed and built in the private sector?
quiz.a: The Rafale, developed by private firms under government research contracts.
